title: Dropping Samples That Out-of-Fold Predictions Contradict Recovers Accuracy Lost to Label Noise in Linear Classifiers
insight: A sample that a linear model fit on the other folds contradicts is mostly a mislabeled sample, so dropping it and refitting wins back much of the accuracy that symmetric label noise costs, with no clean validation set and no noise-rate estimate.
abstract_sketch: Label noise quietly costs even simple classifiers many accuracy points, and the usual remedies need a clean validation set, a noise-rate estimate, or a deep network, none of which a practitioner with a small tabular or image set can count on. We present an out-of-fold disagreement filter: fit logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation on the noisy labels, drop every training sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its label, and refit on the rest. The key idea is that a sample the other folds cannot explain is more likely mislabeled than one they explain. On two small datasets with symmetric noise up to 40%, the filter beats plain logistic regression and an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels, and most of the samples it drops are truly mislabeled. With clean labels it costs under a quarter of a point. This is a small study of linear models, and we make no claim about deep networks or large data.
figure1: Three panels with numbered circles and one to three words per label. Panel 1 'Noisy training set': a grid of colored points (two classes) with a few flipped labels outlined in red. Panel 2 'Out-of-fold check': five folds, each predicted by a model fit on the other four; samples whose predicted label differs from the given label are crossed out; the crossed-out points are mostly the red-outlined ones (precision shown as a small bar). Panel 3 'Refit and test': a grouped bar chart of test accuracy at 40% noise for digits and breast cancer with bars for plain logistic regression, MLP, and our filter (purple), plus a gray marker for logistic regression at 0% noise as the clean reference. Error bars are sd over 5 seeds with individual seed points. A reader sees the problem (noise drops the bars), the idea (cross out what other folds contradict) and the result (purple recovers toward the clean line, MLP collapses) without the text.
contributions: We propose a plain out-of-fold disagreement filter for logistic regression that needs no clean validation set and uses no noise rate.

We show on digits and breast cancer with symmetric noise that the filter beats plain logistic regression and an untuned MLP, that most of the samples it drops are truly mislabeled, and that it costs little on clean labels.
We state the scope and the cases where it does not help: one noisy-label cell is unstable, the MLP ties on clean labels, and no deep-network, large-data or other-noise claim is made.
storyline: Label noise degrades even a linear classifier, and the cost grows with the noise rate, yet the known remedies ask for a clean validation set, a noise-rate estimate or a deep model. We ask whether the simplest possible check is enough: let cross-validation say which labels a model cannot explain. The filter fits logistic regression with 5 folds, drops samples whose out-of-fold prediction contradicts their label, and refits. It works because a model trained on other folds has not memorized the sample's label, so disagreement is evidence of a flipped label; we measure this directly as the precision of the dropped set. On digits the filter wins back most of the lost accuracy and the gain grows with noise, and on breast cancer it helps at 40% noise, with the 20% gain not significant at 5 seeds. Under noise it also beats an untuned MLP in every paired run, and on clean labels it costs a fraction of a point. What it changes: for linear models, noise handling can be a one-line, checkable preprocessing step before reaching for tuned or deep alternatives.

sections.title: Method: drop what the other folds contradict
Label noise costs a linear model many points, and the filter wins most of them back on digits
Most of the samples the filter drops are truly mislabeled
The filtered linear model beats an untuned MLP under noise
On clean labels the filter costs little and the MLP ties it

risks: A reviewer will say the study is tiny (two small datasets, 5 seeds, symmetric noise only) and that confident learning already uses out-of-fold predictions. The paper answers by stating the scope up front (setup_scope, no_baselines_no_scaling), by reporting paired tests and CIs, and by saying plainly that we run no confident-learning or co-teaching comparison. Second, 'recovers most of the loss' is not true on breast cancer at 40% noise (about 22%, with sd near 9 points), and the 20% gain there is not significant; the paper says so and uses the weak claims only with those limits. Third, the MLP is untuned and its collapse is not explained by any experiment; we present it as a baseline result and not as proof of memorization. Fourth, the clean-label cost is not proven zero with 5 seeds, the filter still drops some clean samples, and it costs about five times the fit time.
